title: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. v. Nicastro
lead: A British manufacturer builds a national sales channel, and one confirmed machine sale injures a New Jersey worker. The courts disagree whether seeking American customers establishes the necessary New Jersey connection.

actors.name: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd.
actors.role: English machinery designer and manufacturer, called McIntyre UK.

actors.name: McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd.
actors.role: Separately owned and controlled exclusive U.S. distributor.

actors.name: Curcio Scrap Metal
actors.role: Saddle Brook, New Jersey employer that purchased the shear.

actors.name: Robert Nicastro
actors.role: Injured worker; sued individually and as administrator of Roseanne Nicastro’s estate.

proceedings: The trial court dismissed on March 5, 2004; an unpublished May 26, 2005 appeal allowed jurisdictional discovery.
The trial court dismissed again on November 3, 2006; the Appellate Division reversed on April 9, 2008.
The New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed jurisdiction on February 2, 2010, and remanded for merits proceedings.
The U.S. Supreme Court reversed, six to three, on June 27, 2011, without a majority rationale or an express remand in its disposition.
limits: This account transforms the historical canonical brief, without a fresh opinion audit. The record did not establish four New Jersey sales; Breyer treated one as shown. Defect and damages remained undecided. The Court did not expressly resolve a Marks rule for the fractured opinions, and the federal national-contacts and modern-distribution questions remained open.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: McIntyre UK seeks American buyers through an independent distributor
sections.cue: How did the national sales arrangement work?
paragraphs: J. McIntyre Machinery, Ltd. designed and manufactured metal-recycling machinery in England. It appointed McIntyre Machinery America, Ltd., a separately owned and controlled company, as its exclusive United States distributor. The distributor would promote and sell throughout the country. The state appellate record described an exclusive arrangement without a written agreement, not a produced and signed national-distributorship contract.

McIntyre UK officials joined the distributor at annual conventions in Chicago, Las Vegas, New Orleans, Orlando, San Diego and San Francisco; none was in New Jersey. The distributor followed the manufacturer’s direction and guidance in advertising and sales when possible. Correspondence suggested that some inventory remained the manufacturer’s property until sale, functioning as consigned stock. McIntyre UK held United States and European patents, described worldwide use in its materials, used hydraulic components available internationally, and directed operators to United States safety standards. It deliberately sought the American market.

Curcio Scrap Metal encountered the Model 640 Shear at a Las Vegas recycling convention in 1994 or 1995. Curcio bought it from McIntyre America in 1995 for $24,900, and the distributor shipped it from Ohio to Curcio’s workplace in Saddle Brook, New Jersey.

sources.pinpoint: Parties; Material Facts; 399 N.J. Super. 545–549; 564 U.S. 893–902

sections.title: The shear injures Nicastro and he sues in New Jersey
sections.cue: Which injuries and product defects were alleged?
paragraphs: On October 11, 2001, the three-ton Model 640 Shear severed four fingers from Robert Nicastro’s right hand while he operated it at Curcio Scrap Metal. Nicastro alleged that the machine lacked a safety guard. In September 2003 he filed in the Superior Court of New Jersey, Law Division, Bergen County, asserting defective design and inadequate warnings and seeking medical expenses, lost wages, pain damages and other compensation. He appeared individually and as administrator of Roseanne Nicastro’s estate.

McIntyre UK moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The dispute at this stage concerned New Jersey’s authority to decide the claim against the English manufacturer, not whether the shear was defective or how much Nicastro should recover.

sections.title: Discovery and two appeals produce conflicting assessments of the contacts
sections.cue: What evidence was established, and what remained unproved?
paragraphs: The trial court dismissed on March 5, 2004, finding insufficient contacts under conventional doctrine and even the broadest stream-of-commerce approach it considered. In an unpublished May 26, 2005 decision, the Appellate Division reversed to permit jurisdictional discovery under traditional contacts doctrine, New Jersey’s Charles Gendler rule and O’Connor’s Asahi approach. Those dates and the unpublished appeal’s role come from the later published appellate account.

After discovery, the trial court dismissed again on November 3, 2006. It treated the machine’s arrival as the manufacturer’s only New Jersey connection and found no demonstrated expectation of purchases and use there. McIntyre UK had no New Jersey office or property, paid no taxes there, and neither advertised nor sent employees there. Its convention activity occurred elsewhere; the distributor made the Curcio sale.

The eventual Supreme Court plurality described no more than four machines as reaching New Jersey but said the record suggested only one, the accident machine. An investigator’s unsworn report concerning another machine drew a hearsay objection and a dispute over whether that machine had been sold into New Jersey. Neither the dissent’s note nor the preserved state decisions report an exclusion ruling. The record therefore did not establish four sales. Likewise, absence of introduced evidence of a customer list, regular sales or targeting was not an affirmative finding that no such list or other sale ever existed; no tax payments did not establish the absence of every conceivable tax obligation.

On April 9, 2008, Judge Lisa, joined by Judges Cuff and Simonelli, reversed for the Appellate Division. The court found O’Connor’s stream-of-commerce-plus approach satisfied by the exclusive national distributorship, United States conventions, design for American standards and the sale produced through that arrangement. New Jersey’s workplace-safety interest and the local witnesses and evidence also supported jurisdiction.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History; Material Facts; Source verification; 399 N.J. Super. 544–549, 554–565; 564 U.S. 878, 888–889, 898–899 n.3

sections.title: The state Supreme Court adopts a nationwide-distribution rule
sections.cue: What premise did the United States Supreme Court later reject?
paragraphs: After granting certification, the New Jersey Supreme Court affirmed on February 2, 2010, and remanded for merits proceedings. Justice Albin wrote for Chief Justice Rabner and Justices Long, LaVecchia and Wallace. A foreign manufacturer could be sued, the court reasoned, when it knew or reasonably should have known that its nationwide distribution system might produce sales in any state and took no reasonable step to exclude New Jersey.

Justice Hoens dissented, joined by Justice Rivera-Soto, who also wrote separately. The source brief records those alignments without supplying further details of their reasoning. The actual court opinion identifies Albin and the February 2 decision date; an ancillary website checklist’s contrary date and per-curiam label did not control.

McIntyre UK obtained certiorari. After argument on January 11, 2011, the U.S. Supreme Court divided into a four-Justice plurality, a two-Justice concurrence in the judgment and a three-Justice dissent.

sources.pinpoint: Procedural History; Vote, disposition and source verification; 201 N.J. 48, 987 A.2d 575 (2010)

sections.title: Kennedy requires purposeful affiliation with New Jersey’s sovereign authority
sections.cue: Why were national marketing efforts insufficient for the plurality?
paragraphs: Justice Kennedy, joined by Chief Justice Roberts and Justices Scalia and Thomas, described personal jurisdiction as a sovereign’s authority to bind a defendant. In an ordinary products case, purposeful availment of that sovereign’s benefits and protections provided the necessary affiliation. Because this suit was in state court, the relevant sovereign was New Jersey.

The national distributor, conventions elsewhere and limited evidence of New Jersey machines showed a desire for United States sales, but did not establish the manufacturer’s purposeful submission to New Jersey. The plurality identified no New Jersey-directed advertisement, employee visit, shipment, office, property, tax payment or other act invoking New Jersey law. It would require forum-directed conduct beyond pursuit of the national market.

The plurality reserved whether Congress could authorize federal jurisdiction under the Fifth Amendment based on aggregate national contacts. Its sovereignty and targeting approach had four votes, not a majority.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: Kennedy plurality and application; 564 U.S. 877–887

sections.title: Breyer reaches the same result on the limited record
sections.cue: What broader rules did the decisive concurring Justices decline to adopt?
paragraphs: Justice Breyer, joined by Justice Alito, relied on existing precedent and the evidence Nicastro had introduced. World-Wide Volkswagen rejected jurisdiction based on an isolated product arrival. Asahi’s separate opinions pointed toward a regular sales flow, additional forum-related conduct, or significant volume, value and hazard. Nicastro bore the burden and showed one isolated sale, without proving a regular New Jersey flow or a particular New Jersey sales effort. On that record Breyer voted to reverse.

Breyer declined both Kennedy’s broader sovereignty theory and New Jersey’s automatic national-distribution rule. This limited record did not require decisions about high-volume nationwide sales, direct internet sales, fulfillment by a large intermediary, or website advertising known to reach the forum. He also considered the implications of broad automatic jurisdiction for small foreign enterprises.

Six Justices therefore voted to reverse on two distinct rationales. The concurrence’s narrower factual reasoning cannot be recast as an expressly declared generally controlling Marks holding: the opinion did not decide that question. Nor did the five Justices who declined Kennedy’s approach thereby adopt a shared alternative rule. The assigned textbook’s Marks discussion asks students to analyze the fractured decision rather than announcing another holding.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: Breyer, open questions, precedential rule; Source verification; 564 U.S. 887–893

sections.title: Ginsburg treats the New Jersey sale as the intended distribution system at work
sections.cue: Why did the dissent distinguish World-Wide Volkswagen and Asahi?
paragraphs: Justice Ginsburg, joined by Justices Sotomayor and Kagan, would sustain jurisdiction. McIntyre UK hired a distributor to develop the whole United States, attended conventions, adapted its product for American use and sought revenue wherever American buyers lived. New Jersey was part of that cultivated market. The distributor delivered the shear there through the very commercial system the manufacturer established, and the product caused the local injury underlying the suit.

World-Wide Volkswagen involved a consumer carrying a locally sold car into Oklahoma, without forum-directed conduct by the dealer or regional distributor. Here a national distribution arrangement generated the forum sale. Asahi concerned a component supplier with limited control and, after settlement, a foreign indemnity dispute. McIntyre UK actively sought American customers and faced a local worker’s claim at the place of sale and injury. Ginsburg’s appendix supplied twelve illustrative decisions sustaining jurisdiction over manufacturers using national distributors, qualified as nonexhaustive; it was an appendix of cases, not promotional material.

On June 27, 2011, the Court reversed six to three. The formal disposition did not add an express remand. That judgment defeated New Jersey jurisdiction over McIntyre UK on this record, without deciding defect or damages. The plurality, concurrence and dissent remain separately attributed routes through the distribution problem; modern sales practices and possible federal alternatives remained unresolved.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: Ginsburg and precedent distinctions; Vote, disposition and source verification; 564 U.S. 887, 893–914
